findings.title: Device limit can be bypassed after first rejection because local cache is set before validation
findings.body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for an unknown device, the cache entry is not removed. On the next request for the same device ID within the cache TTL (29 minutes), tagDeviceUI returns nil from the cache and Authenticate proceeds without checking the limit. As a result, a rejected anonymous device can immediately retry and authenticate, defeating the configured device limit. Cache should only be populated after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or the entry should be invalidated on error.

findings.title: Device limit check is not atomic with insert
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate CountDevices query and then, if count < deviceLimit, executes an INSERT/UPDATE without any transaction or locking. Concurrent anonymous authentication requests can all observe count < limit and all insert new devices, allowing the configured anonymousDeviceLimit to be exceeded. Use a transaction with appropriate locking or an atomic conditional insert to enforce the limit.

findings.title: MySQL zero affected rows can falsely trigger ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device
findings.body: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, an UPDATE that matches an existing row but does not change any column values (or only changes values within timestamp precision) returns 0 affected rows by default because the server reports changed rows rather than matched rows. When a device is already stored with the same client_ip and user_agent and the updated_at value resolves to the same stored value (for example, within the same second), updateDevice may return ErrDeviceLimitReached even though the device is within the active window and should be allowed. This causes intermittent authentication failures for existing devices under the limit, especially in multi-instance deployments that do not share the local cache.

findings.title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on a database write for every new device
findings.body: Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget TagDevice in a goroutine with a timeout to a synchronous call using the request context. Even when AnonymousDeviceLimit is 0 (the default), every first request for a device on each Grafana instance performs a synchronous DB INSERT/UPDATE in CreateOrUpdateDevice before authentication returns. This adds database latency to anonymous login and reintroduces the DB as a dependency on the auth hot path that the previous async timeout was designed to avoid. Consider keeping the write asynchronous when no limit is configured, or otherwise constrain the synchronous path to only the operations needed to enforce a limit.

findings.title: No test for an existing device when limit is reached or cache failure bypass
findings.body: The new test only covers two distinct new devices exceeding the limit. It does not cover updating an existing active device when the limit is already reached (which should succeed), nor does it exercise the local-cache path in impl.go where a limit rejection leaves the cache populated and permits the next attempt. These cases are important because both are places where the current implementation has edge cases.
